issues.legal_issue: Implementing an arbitral award that fixes an uncertain and disputed boundary does not require a constitutional amendment when it does not cede territory established to be part of the country.
material_facts: The two governments agreed to refer their conflicting claims about the boundary to a tribunal and undertook to implement its binding decision.
The terrain was shifting and difficult to demarcate, and the parties had not established a clear, mutually accepted boundary in the disputed areas.

The claim maps and historical material were conflicting, and there was no reliable evidence that the disputed areas had been part of the former state or had been subject to its sovereign administration.
The award determined the boundary’s alignment; the limited presence of security personnel and a polling booth did not establish territorial administration.
The challengers did not ask the court to reject the award, which the government had accepted.
issues.conclusion: The award settled a disputed boundary rather than ceding established national territory, so the executive could implement it without a constitutional amendment.
issues.legal_principle: Articles 1 and 3, Article 73, Article 253, and Entries 14 and 15 of List I inform the allocation of authority over territory, treaties, and executive action. Cession of territory established as part of India requires a constitutional amendment, as held in In re Berubari Union and Exchange of Enclaves (the first Berubari case). Transfer of territory that had not become Indian territory did not require one, as held in Ram Kishore Sen v. Union of India (the second Berubari case). Fixing an uncertain boundary through an agreed process is distinct from ceding known national territory; ordinarily, the executive may implement a valid boundary adjustment unless a clear case of cession is involved.

rule.if: boundary_award_implementation and boundary_referred_for_determination and boundary_indefinite and not established_home_territory

predicates.boundary_award_implementation: The proceeding challenges the government's implementation of an arbitral award determining an international boundary.
predicates.boundary_referred_for_determination: The governments concerned referred competing boundary claims to an agreed decision-maker and undertook to implement the decision.
predicates.boundary_indefinite: The boundary had not been clearly and reliably demarcated, and the relevant terrain or evidence left its location uncertain.
predicates.established_home_territory: Reliable evidence establishes that the territory at issue was part of the country before the boundary was determined.

issues.definition: When a challenge concerns implementation of an award on a referred boundary and the boundary was indefinite without reliable proof that the affected territory was part of the country, the executive may implement the award without a constitutional amendment.

issues.legal_issue: The executive may implement an international agreement without legislation when implementation neither changes domestic law nor restricts or infringes justiciable rights.
material_facts: The government had undertaken to implement the tribunal’s binding award and accepted it as an international obligation.
The disputed territory had no local residents, private property, or agriculture.
The claimed effects on citizens concerned movement and residence in territory that had not been established as Indian territory.
issues.conclusion: The agreement and award bound the governments internationally, but legislation was not required to implement them in this case because no domestic law was modified and no justiciable rights were shown to be affected.
issues.legal_principle: Article 73 gives the Union executive power over matters within Parliament’s legislative competence and the exercise of authority arising under treaties; Article 253 confers legislative power on Parliament to implement international agreements but does not limit the executive power conferred by Article 73. Entries 10 and 14 of List I concern foreign affairs and treaties. The court applied the distinction between making a treaty and performing obligations that require changes to domestic law, discussed in Attorney-General for Canada v. Attorney-General for Ontario, and referred to The Parlement Belge and Walker v. Baird. A treaty does not by itself bind individuals under domestic law; legislation is required when performance changes domestic law or restricts or infringes justiciable rights.

rule.if: treaty_implementation_case and executive_treaty_commitment and not domestic_law_changed and not justiciable_rights_affected

predicates.treaty_implementation_case: The proceeding concerns the domestic implementation of an international agreement or award.
predicates.executive_treaty_commitment: The executive entered an international commitment and undertook to perform it.
predicates.domestic_law_changed: Implementation changes or modifies domestic law.
predicates.justiciable_rights_affected: Implementation restricts or infringes rights enforceable by individuals in domestic courts.

issues.definition: When the executive has undertaken to perform an international commitment, it may implement that commitment without legislation if implementation neither changes domestic law nor affects justiciable rights.
